title: How Long
year_note: A UK single on Anchor in 1974 (it was in the UK chart by November that year). The US release came in March 1975, and it peaked at 3 there in 1975.

notes.made: Paul Carrack wrote it and sings it, and plays the keyboards. Ace first tried to cut it as a Motown-style single for Anchor, gave up, and made it part of their debut album instead, produced by John Anthony at Rockfield in Wales (Trident in London also gets a credit). Phil Harris plays the guitar solo, Alan 'Bam' King rhythm guitar, Terry 'Tex' Comer bass and Fran Byrne drums.
notes.context: Most people hear a cheating song. Carrack wrote it after finding out that Comer had been secretly working with the Sutherland Brothers and Quiver, so the betrayal is about a band, not a lover. It reached 20 in the UK and 3 in the US and Canada, and the album went to 11 on the Billboard 200. In March 2020 an Amazon Prime advert put it back at number 1 on Billboard's Rock Digital Song Sales chart, and in 2025 the Horne Section played it for 24 hours straight for charity.

listen_for.note: Phil Harris, the band's lead guitarist, kept short and melodic so it never pulls focus from Carrack's voice.
Carrack's keyboards (he's credited with organ, piano and electric piano) carry the groove with Comer's bass. Lipps Inc. and Aswad with Yazz both turned it into dance records later.

leads_to.title: How Long
leads_to.why: The disco cover, which reached 4 on the US dance chart and sold a million in Mexico.

notes.unverified: I couldn't confirm an exact UK release date, and I couldn't confirm which keyboard plays which part.

culture.title: Top 3 in America
culture.line: Reached 3 in the US and Canada and 20 in the UK. Phil Collins put it in his top 10 in Smash Hits in 1981.

culture.title: Amazon Prime advert
culture.line: After an Amazon Prime ad in March 2020 it went to number 1 on Billboard's Rock Digital Song Sales, with sales up more than 2,000%.

culture.title: Lipps Inc. and Rod Stewart
culture.line: Lipps Inc. took it to 4 on the US dance chart in 1980, and Rod Stewart charted with it in 1981.
